newsitem.title: USA: Lower Calif. electricity rates not expected soon.
newsitem.headline: Lower Calif. electricity rates not expected soon.

text.p: California's biggest power users will have a hard time trimming their bills any time soon, despite the state's plan to allow competition among retail power suppliers next year, industry experts said at a recent conference.

"It will be a challenge to get a substantial reduction in rates in the first four years," said Gregory Conlon, president of the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC), speaking at municipal utilities conference here on Friday.

This is because by January the "commodity" price of electricity--the market segment undergoing deregulation--is expected to make up only about 30 percent of the price at the bottom of the electricity bill, he and others explained.
"Even if you got the energy for free, you would only see a 25 percent rate cut," noted Wayne Sakarias, restructuring manager at Enova Corp's San Diego Gas & Electric Co.
Furthermore, during California's four-year transition to full competition, the CPUC has ordered more costly plants, including nuclear units, to continue running.
Under California's restructuring plan, distribution costs, which will continue to be a monopoly business regulated by the CPUC, will still be the biggest component in power prices.
The next highest cost will be the "competitive transition charge," or CTC, which will be levied on all California electricity buyers between next January and the end of 2002.

CTC revenues will be used to pay off up to $25 billion in investor-owned utility stranded costs, such as nuclear plant investments and power purchase contracts which are likely to be unprofitable under a competitive market.
Other bill items will be a three percent charge for "public goods programs" and charges for long-distance transmission.
Under California's plan, residential and small commerical customers are guaranteed a 10 percent rate cut for the four-year transition period.
The rate cut will be financed by debt securities, backed by CTC revenues, which will have a 10-year re-payment period.
"After 2002 there will be no utility generation (included) in your rates," said John Fielder, vice president of regulatory policy at Edison International's Southern California Edison Co.
With the generation component of rates expected to offer thin profit margins, "the real play will be in products and services to customers," SDG&E's Sakarias said.
In addition, "conservation is also cost effective," noted Nancy Day, vice president of cusomer services and New Energy Ventures Inc.
"You don't spend any of it (rate components) if you don't use that kilowatt hour," she said.
CPUC president Conlon emphasized the best way to cut power bills will be to "reduce usage or re-schedule it."
He believes many customers will act to use more power during low-cost overnight hours and less during high-cost daytime hours when rates change to reflect those costs.
David Freeman, trustee of California's power exchange and independent system operators board, also stressed "people don't pay rates, they pay bills. Conservation will be needed."
"Anyone who thinks there is going to a huge price reduction come January 1 is living on another planet," he said.
((--D Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761))
